stories.body:
Deference was deafening as US president rolled out red carpet for world’s biggest jailer of journalists – perhaps he was seeking tips

One is an authoritarian who represses the media and has a strong allergy to democratic elections. The other is head of the Chinese Communist party.

Donald Trump welcomed the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to the White House on Thursday, setting the stage for a scene quite unlike anything the august old building has seen over more than two centuries.

“Remarkably,” observed the US president, “this is our first time meeting together here at the White House, and as President Xi has already seen, a lot has changed since he was last here.”

While Xi remained poker-faced, only a brief look around a grand foyer bedecked with American and Chinese flags would have verified Trump’s statement. On one wall, where an official portrait of Barack Obama once hung, was the dramatic image of a bloodied Trump with fist raised urging his supporters to “fight!” after a failed assassination attempt.

And while Chinese state media had been welcomed onto the White House grounds, many US journalists had not, thanks to Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico. Michael McFaul, a former US diplomat, described the vivid contrast as “wrong and embarrassing”.

That was hard to deny, given that China ranks 178th in Reporters Without Borders’ press freedom index, ahead of only North Korea and Eritrea (the US, for the record, is down to 64th). But it also made perfect sense because, whereas past presidents sought to make China more like the US, Trump evidently aspires to make the US more like China.

The deference was deafening. On Wednesday night he and his wife, Melania, travelled to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to greet Xi off his plane – a schlep that US presidents rarely make for foreign leaders – and rolled out a literal red carpet for his strongman soulmate.

Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, observed on X : “If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll roll out the red carpet for you…”

Vladimir, are you feeling jealous yet?

“I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit — Better than ever,” a gooey-eyed Trump gushed on his Truth Social patform. “Madam Xi, of course, BEAUTIFUL!”

Protocol error! Protocol error! When the president wrote “Madam Xi”, referring to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, he should have said “Madame Peng”, which is how she is recognised.

Xi is such a star that he got two welcomes. On Thursday morning, there were more flags, more trumpet blasts, and another red carpet as the Trumps emerged from the White House south portico to greet Xi and Peng.

Then it was on to the grand foyer for statements – with no reporter questions allowed, of course – before the two delegations, including Vice-President JD Vance and wife Usha, sitting in neat rows. Trump went first. You can tell when he’s on his best behaviour because he (mostly) sticks to the teleprompter. The interpreter must have been relieved that he did not have to match Trump, weave for weave.

Trump touted his “truly ⁠great friendship” with Xi and claimed the two countries ⁠had made strides on trade since his trip ​to China in May. “During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and ‘super intelligence,’” he said, using his alternative name for artificial intelligence. If Xi felt like rolling his eyes at that, he managed to resist.

The president, ever nostalgic for the 20th century, suggested that the second world war offers a lesson on how the competitors can work together. “Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country,” he said, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that helped defend China against Japanese invasion. “They were just unbelievable.”

He added that it was US marines’ interactions with Chinese citizens that inspired them “to adopt a Chinese phrase that they still use today: gung ho”.

Rarely does Trump appear at an event and not end up behind the microphone for longer than any other speaker on the bill.

But it was Xi, speaking more substantially, who looked like he owned the place. Trump, sitting behind with hands clasped together, had the appearance of junior partner. Xi said he was ready to work with the president to “steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future”.

Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!

Xi had a charm offensive of his own. “President Trump and I have respect for each other,” he said. “We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”

He announced Thursday that 100,000 young American students would be invited to study in China over the next five years. Better still, he revealed China will send two giant pandas – Ping Ping and Fuchuan – to a zoo in Atlanta.

Then he got to the meat in the sandwich, insisting that the countries can “co-exist in peace” and their competition “should be a healthy one”. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi declared, in a tacit acknowledgement that China is threatening to displace the US as the world’s superpower.

But with more flattery, he added: “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand.”

Next up was a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden, with Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof alongside US flags. A marching band dressed in the garb of the Revolutionary War era – tricorn hats, white wigs, red tunics – paraded in the paved over Rose Garden (another change since Xi’s last visit).

None of this was covered by the usual cable news networks because they were boycotting shared coverage, in solidarity with the banned outlets. If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound? If a democracy falls and no one is around to film it, does it make a yelp?

Trump then sat down with the world’s biggest jailer of journalists for bilateral talks. Perhaps he was seeking tips.

When they met face to face, was this a Reagan-Gorbachev style summit of great historical import, discussing guardrails on AI and other ways not to destroy the world? Maybe not.

Showing off the Marine One helicopter and his new helipad on the south lawn, Trump reported : “We had a great meeting - and he has a great interest in granite. He likes granite. He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.”

Not even Xi had been spared the dreaded tour of Trump’s architectural follies.

By the afternoon, some of the banned reporters had been allowed back on to the White House campus after a judge found Trump’s action to be unconstitutional. It must have been a tricky one to explain to Xi. He remains the master of repression; Trump is merely The Apprentice.

Increase comes after Fed decision to raise interest rates, as Americans struggle with high prices and stagnant wages

US mortgage rates surpassed 7% for the first time since January 2025, according to federal lender Freddie Mac, aggravating a housing market that has endured years of high interest rates and low supply.

The increase comes after the US Federal Reserve hiked interest rates , which directly affect mortgage rates, for the first time since 2023, citing high inflation.

Rates on 16 September went up by a quarter of a point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%. In new projections, a majority of the Fed’s rate-setting committee predicted at least one additional rate hike before the end of this year.

Last year, the Freddie Mac 30-year-mortgage rate, commonly used on home loans across the country, had been trending down from 7.79% – a generational high reached in late 2023.

But rates have been creeping back up since late February, when the US and Israel launched its war with Iran . The conflict drove inflation to its highest levels in three years and sharply increased energy prices.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, topped $105 earlier on Thursday.

after newsletter promotion

On Thursday, the 10-year US treasury yield – which underpins the 30-year mortgage rate and other borrowing costs – also reached its highest level since July 2007 and the 30-year Treasury yield hitting its peak since 2004 as investors raised expectations for another Fed rate hike next month.

Earlier in September, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent announced the Treasury would triple its buyback of government debt, but yields have continued to rise.

The housing market has long been in a slowdown, said Anthony Smith, a senior economist at Realtor.com , with existing home sales hitting their 2026 low so far in August and pending sales that have turned negative year over year.

“A 7% handle is as much psychological as mathematical, and it arrives at the point in the season when leverage usually shifts toward buyers,” said Smith.

High mortgage rates are just one of the many reasons why Americans are struggling to attain home ownership. Wages have not kept pace with higher inflation, and everyday costs are higher.

The frustration is expected to show up in November’s midterm elections as Republicans struggle to maintain control of Congress. Nearly three-quarters of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, according to a recent CNN poll conducted by SSRS , and two-thirds of registered voters rate the economy as “extremely important” to their vote.

stories.body:
Explosive growth in imported vehicles omitted from EV tariffs fuels concern for future of European carmakers

EU imports three times more from China than bloc exports there

Sales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry.

In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU. However, after Brussels imposed anti-subsidy tariffs on fully electric cars from China in 2024, sales of hybrids have shot up to 160,662 in the first seven months of this year.

Eurostat figures show that sales of Chinese-made plug-in hybrid vehicles – models popular for longer driving distances that can recharge via both the fuel engine and an external power source – have also soared, rising from 56,706 sold in 2022 to 217,764 from January to July this year.

The volume of Chinese hybrids on the roads is now spooking the car industry and Brussels, which has asked China to voluntarily reduce its hybrid exports to the EU or face safeguards, likely to be quotas.

On Thursday the German car industry for the first time indicated it would be willing to consider tariffs on Chinese hybrids specifically.

The German Association of the Automotive Industry, VDA, called on the European Commission to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the impact of any trade safeguards, which can range from quotas to price floors and tariffs.

It said: “The EU must also have an effective and up-to-date set of trade defence instruments at its disposal. Where unfair conduct is proven, the use of WTO-compliant trade defence instruments must be considered; these are legitimate and tried-and-tested means of achieving a level playing field and safeguarding fair conditions of competition.”

According to new figures released by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), hybrid cars now account for almost 37% of the overall market, with electric cars making up just over 21% of the market.

The ACEA figures show three Chinese manufacturers – BYD, Chery and Leapmotor – making significant inroads with triple-digit growth in the EU.

A fourth firm, Geely, has had a steady 8% increase in the first eight months of the year and remains the most popular Chinese brand in the EU, with 205,000 cars sold in the first eight months of the year. Its brands include Sweden’s Volvo and Polestar, the EU’s only all-electric car manufacturer.

BYD is catching up with Geely, with sales rocketing by 163% year on year with 177,000 units sold.

Both firms, along with a fifth Chinese manufacturer, SAIC, are now firmly ahead of Elon Musk’s Tesla, which sold 142,000 cars across the bloc in the first seven months of the year.

European car manufacturers still dominate, with the Volkswagen group selling 2m cars in the first eight months of the year.

after newsletter promotion

Sales of electric cars are also growing fast in parts of Europe including Germany, up 75% to 69,000 units in August, and in France, where sales are up by 112%. In Slovenia, sales have increased by 266%. This compares with the UK, up 27% in August to 28,000 EVs sold, and Ireland, up just 7% to 2,200 units.

Earlier this month, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, described the now €1.18bn-a-day trade deficit between the bloc and China as having reached an unsustainable “tipping point”.

The EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao will meet on 8 and 9 October to try to build a truce.

Also hoping for a trade truce are Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, who meet in their third summit in 12 months in Washington on Thursday.

Trump agreed in South Korea last October to drop tariffs on certain Chinese imports in exchange for a suspension of China’s export restriction on rare earths, critical to the car industry across the US, EU and the UK.

Some believe a deal may not have been reached yet and the suspension may not be announced until the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference next month.

stories.title: Miliband tells Iran minister UK will not tolerate 'hostile activity' on British soil
stories.summary: The foreign secretary stresses "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 25 September 2026, 03:51 BST

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi that the UK will "not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil".

The ministers met face-to-face at the UN General Assembly in New York City.

The Foreign Office said Miliband spoke to his counterpart about "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community". They also discussed war in the Middle East and a British couple detained in Iran, it said.

There was no immediate comment from Araghchi. Iranian news agency Irna reported that the men "discussed bilateral ties and international developments during their talks".

Miliband's comments follow an arson attack on four Jewish community ambulances in Golders Green in March and other incidents.

The BBC understands that UK intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it played a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026.

They later concluded that intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack.

A small power plant in the UK was also shut down in July due to a cyber attack, which the Telegraph reported , external was carried out by hackers affiliated with the Iranian regime.

The Foreign Office said Miliband also spoke to his counterpart about the country's war with the US, telling Araghchi that Iran should choose "de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war" while stressing the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran, killing the country's supreme leader.

Iran responded by launching strikes on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states that host US military bases. It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, impacting the global economy.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly on Wednesday that any peace deal would have to include an end to the US blockade preventing Iranian ships from using the waterway.

Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal was not reached soon, Pezeshkian said his country will never "bend the knee" .

"The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying," he said.

There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address.

The Foreign Office said Miliband also used Thursday's meeting to raise the detention of British couple Lindsay and Craig Foreman .

The couple, from East Sussex, have been detained in Iran for more than 20 months after being arrested while passing through the country on a motorcycle journey.

The Foremans were each sentenced to 10 years in jail in February on espionage charges, which they deny.

In Miliband's discussion with the Iranian foreign minister, he reiterated the call for them to be immediately released and stressed that their welfare remained a priority for the government, the Foreign Office said.

stories.title: Fifteen new members in Isle of Man general election
stories.summary: Three ministers lose their seats and Peel and Glenfaba elects the Isle of Man's youngest MHK.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
First-time MHK Kirrie Jenkins (second right) topped the poll in Arbory, Castletown, and Malew

Published 24 September 2026

Fifteen new members have been elected in the 2026 general election, with three members of the council of ministers losing their seats.

The outgoing enterprise minister Tim Johnston, education, sport and culture minister Daphne Caine and environment, food and agriculture minister Clare Barber have all lost their seats in the House of Keys.

Former infrastructure minister Michelle Haywood, former health and social care minister Lawrie Hooper, former education, sport and culture minister Julie Edge, and deputy speaker of the house Ann Corlett were also among the seven outgoing MHks that were not re-elected.

In the western constituency of Glenfaba and Peel, Daniel Davison said it was "surreal" to be the youngest ever MHK to be elected in Manx politics at the age of 18.

Chief Minister Alfred Cannan kept his seat in Ayre and Michael

There were 82 candidates contesting the election for the 24 seats available in the House of Keys.

The poll saw 15 new Members of the House of Keys selected, eight of whom are women - down from 10 in 2021.

The new House of Keys had been guaranteed to have eight new faces following the retirement from politics of six members, the election of Juan Watterson as President of Tynwald, and the death of John Wannenburgh in August.

The results have seen the re-election of two members of the Manx Labour Party - Sarah Maltby and Joney Faragher.

However Liberal Vannin Party leader Lawrie Hooper losing his seat in Ramsey means that party has no elected MHKs for the first time since it was established. Party founder Peter Karran failed to make a political comeback in Onchan after 10 years away from politics.

Neither of the newly created parties - Change and Transform Isle of Man - secured seats.

Sarah Maltby topped the poll in Douglas South

Elected

Stephen Broad and Alfred Cannan have been elected for Ayre and Michael

In Ayre and Michael, Stephen Broad topped the poll while Chief Minister Alfred Cannan has kept his seat.

Broad told Manx Radio he would "give it my best shot".

Cannan said the election period had been a "humbling experience" but thanked constituents for taking the time to speak to him.

He said he needed to shape things in a way to try to address some of the "critical problems that have been raised on the doorstep and that "we all know we are facing".

The result meant former Enterprise Minister Tim Johnston was ousted from his seat.

Katryna Baptist and Daniel Davison have been elected in Glenfaba and Peel

In Glenfaba and Peel, Katryna Baptist came out on top, with Daniel Davison becoming the youngest ever person to be elected to the House of Keys.

Baptist told Manx Radio she was "really excited" although there was a "lot of work to do".

Davison, who is 18, said it was "such a surreal experience," adding that "it brings a generation to government who have never been there before".

Jane Poole-Wilson and James Cochrane have been elected for Middle

Deputy Chief Minister Jane Poole-Wilson attracted the most votes in Middle, with James Cochraine taking the other seat.

Poole-Wilson told Manx Radio that she was "honoured" to be re-elected and to have served over the past five years.

James Cochrane said he was "really proud" to have stood next to the other candidates in Middle.

In Douglas East, Andy Saunders and Joney Faragher have been elected

In Douglas East, Andy Saunders came out on top of the poll while Joney Faragher kept her seat.

But Environment, Food and Agriculture Minister Clare Barber was out after 10 years in the House of Keys.

Richard Henthorn and Victoria Hewison have been elected for Garff

Richard Henthorn and Victoria Hewison have been elected for Garff.

Reacting to the results, Hewison said she was "shocked" as she "really didn't expect to get in".

Kirrie Jenkins and Jason Moorhouse will represent Arbory, Castletown and Malew

Kirrie Jenkins and Jason Moorhouse will represent Arbory, Castletown and Malew.

Jenkins said she was feeling "elation" to be elected and she was "speechless".

And Moorhouse said it was a "privilege" to be elected for a third term.

Juan McGuinness topped the poll followed by Robert Cowell

Juan McGuinness topped the poll in Ramsey followed by Robert Cowell.

McGuinness told Manx Radio that the "hard work starts now," and Robert Cowell said he was "overwhelmed" and "very grateful" to be elected.

Lawrie Hooper, who lost his seat after 10 years in the House of Keys, said that although he was "disappointed" McGuinness and Cowell would do a "fantastic job".

Hooper, who is a former health minister, said he was proud of his work to reduce waiting lists, and would now go back to being a chartered accountant.

David Ashford and Damian Ciappelli will represent Douglas North

In Douglas North, David Ashford topped the poll for the third time, while Damian Ciappelli was elected to the seat previously held by John Wannenburgh, who died suddenly in August.

Ciappelli told Manx Radio that he was "delighted" to be elected and was "ready to get stuck in."

Peter Shimmin tops the poll in Douglas Central followed by Chris Thomas

Peter Shimmin, who secured the highest number of votes in Douglas Central, said he was "overwhelmed" and "incredibly grateful".

When asked about his priorities, he said the economy, affordable housing and "anything that supports younger people and families and makes the Isle of Man a great place to build your future".

Current Treasury Minister Chris Thomas – who kept his seat – said he was "very pleased" to be elected in a "difficult constituency".

He said there were "many, many important challenges and we need to rise to them", citing issues with transport, public finances, healthcare and food security.

"Compromise is a good thing, consensus is a good thing, but we can't afford a fudge," he added.

Meanwhile, Ann Corlett, who lost her seat, said it was "a little disappointing" but she had "a strange sense of relief" that she could "get back" to her life and "do some of the things I've been planning to do".

She said her highlights included bringing through social legislation and being Deputy Speaker of the House of Keys.

Mark Kemp and Michael Crowe have been elected in Rushen

Michael Crowe and Mark Kemp were elected in Rushen, while former infrastructure minister Michelle Haywood lost her seat.

Crowe, who topped the poll, said he was "grateful" to be elected and was "looking forward to getting stuck in".

Kemp told Manx Radio: "I think people are just sick of what we've had," adding that he wanted to focus on diversifying the economy.

Rob Callister said on Facebook that he was "deeply grateful and honoured" to have been re-elected, adding, "tomorrow, I get back to work".

Julie Edge, who failed to get re-elected, told Manx Radio: "I have worked really hard for the people of Onchan, and I have delivered, but the results are what they are."

Edge, who served a spell as education minister during the outgoing administration, said she would continue with her work on whistleblowing.

Sarah Maltby and Claire Christian have both been re-elected in Douglas South

In Douglas South, Claire Christian said she was "really thrilled" with the "really wonderful" result.

Christian, who is the current health minister, added: "I want to thank the electorate."

Sarah Maltby, who topped the poll for a second time, said on social media: "Thank you for trusting me to represent Douglas South.

"I am completely overwhelmed with the support."

Peter Shimmin topped the poll in Douglas Central, followed by Chris Thomas

What's next?

Those who have been elected will be sworn in as MHKs on Tuesday by the first and second deemsters.

The House of Keys will then sit on 13 October to nominate a chief minister and speaker of the House of Keys.

stories.title: New policies, election speculation: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM
stories.summary: Andy Burnham is under pressure to deliver a compelling vision for the country as he steps from the sidelines on to the main stage.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Andy Burnham is gearing up to deliver his first conference speech as Labour leader

Published 25 September 2026, 00:44 BST

Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool.

But that was at a fringe meeting on the sidelines of the main event.

Now, as Labour leader and prime minister, he is the main event - and it is down to him to show party members and the wider public that he has some answers.

Earlier this week, he said his debut leader's speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role".

"People are going to know the direction I want to take this country and I will set it down quite clearly," he told reporters en route to the UN General Assembly in New York.

An internal No 10 note has set out the broad themes he will explore when he takes to the stage in Liverpool on Tuesday - including setting out long-term solutions to build a belief that the future can be brighter.

The slogan for this year's conference is "Hope Again".

So in his speech he is likely to point to his forthcoming 10 Year Plan for the UK – which, he says, will have "making life more affordable" at its core.

As for the specifics of what he will say, some of it will be very familiar to anyone who was listening to his conference fringe speech 12 months ago.

Potential crowd-pleaser

Back then, he declared then that the country had "lost control" of "the essentials" following the Thatcher-era sell off of utilities and that we were all "overpaying for water, housing energy, transport".

He called for a renewed emphasis on technical education and wanted to see a decade of council house building on the scale of the post-war Labour government.

For a politician frequently denounced for "flip flopping" he has been remarkably consistent in recent times.

He is likely to re-alight on themes from his Labour leadership campaign – saying more about his commitment to greater "public control" – though not necessarily public ownership - of life's necessities; building national resilience in an unstable world; and investing political capital in the reform of social care.

A potential crowd pleaser would be to tell Labour activists from the main stage what he told them as Greater Manchester mayor from the fringe last year – that he will set up a commission to examine electoral reform.

A quarter of his own MPs signed a parliamentary amendment calling for this, and the Labour conference has previously given its backing to changing the voting system, though this was not taken forward in government.

But it may now be a way of demonstrating Burnham's commitment to a "new politics".

We are also likely to hear more about getting young people into work or training, with the conclusions of the review by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn likely to be published soon.

And there is certain to be plenty about his efforts to devolve power away from Whitehall to England's mayors and the new No 10 North.

The task for Burnham is to meld these snapshots into a compelling and coherent narrative, culminating in a vision of the Britain he wants to see a decade from now.

But there are already worries that this might become a fictional narrative unless he also focuses even more on the here and now.

After all, Sir Keir Starmer's "decade of national renewal" was binned after just two bumpy years in office.

Unite's Sharon Graham is calling for more help with the cost of living

We are told there will be policy announcements on each day of the conference – starting on Saturday.

Each announcement will have to fit in with the PM's priorities – "putting power in people's hands" - in other words more devolved powers; "growth in every postcode" – such as investment decisions around the country; and help with cost of living.

Windfall tax?

Party insiders say measures such as removing VAT from electricity bills are just the start of that assistance.

But Labour's biggest union funder, Unite, wants to see much more robust action on living costs sooner rather than later. The union does not want the promise of jam tomorrow, but some instant sweeteners.

Its leader, Sharon Graham, has called for a "winter fuel in reverse" – a policy from Burnham next week which would be as popular as Starmer's early removal of payments from many pensioners was unpopular.

The union has put forward a motion which gives the PM plenty of options such as a cap on energy prices and unfreezing tax thresholds – an issue Burnham himself said had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to be the MP for Makerfield.

The union has said revenue can be raised through a windfall tax on banks. The umbrella body for unions, the TUC, has called for an increase in the bank surcharge to subsidise energy bills.

All eyes will be on John Healey's first conference speech as chancellor on Monday.

With borrowing costs for last month soaring to their second highest level , his room for manoeuvre is limited and he will not scoop his own Budget next month by announcing what is in it.

But Labour activists will be keen to know from his language whether Healey's Treasury will opt for continuity or will represent a break from the past two years under Rachel Reeves, not just in rhetoric but reality.

Early election?

Some in Labour's ranks believe Burnham is planning for an early election, with party HQ recently launching "operation second term", to beef up its campaigning and organising strength.

Burnham does not have to call an election until August 2029 - but going to the country early - perhaps as early as next spring - could deliver him a mandate of his own and free him from the constraints of Sir Keir Starmer's 2024 manifesto.

Recent polling has suggested that a "Burnham bounce" is real, though not dramatic.

The party has moved from just under 20% in the polls at the end of the Starmer era to around the mid-twenties now.

Ipsos puts its standing as high as 28% , external , while YouGov registers a more modest 23% , external .

Labour strategists will be pleased that Reform UK's share – 21% in YouGov - is the lowest since January 2025, and that Nigel Farage's party is now neck-and-neck with Kemi Badenoch's Conservatives.

One Labour insider told me that Burnham is happy to see a resilient Badenoch, as this blunts Reform support and could point to a split vote on the right at an election.

And new research from YouGov , external suggests that at the all important constituency level, 63-68% of Lib Dem and Green voters would tactically vote for Labour to stop Reform UK winning their seat.

Burnham of course also faces a challenge on the left.

How much of a threat Zack Polanski's Greens can be in some traditional Labour seats will be tested in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election just a week after the Labour conference concludes.

Downing Street insists that an early election is not being planned.

To say anything else, though, would be to repeat the uncertainty of Gordon Brown's early months in No 10 when election speculation wasn't doused - and had become so rife that he was reputationally damaged when he decided not to go to the polls.

But some who have been in regular touch with No 10 tell me they have seen no serious signs that an early election is in the offing.

Burnham appears determined to give his government enough time in office to present tangible achievements to a sceptical electorate.

And with Labour still well below the 34% vote share it captured in 2024, many Labour MPs will be pushing the PM not to cut and run.

So don't expect the centre point of Burnham's conference speech to be a message to his MPs to go back to their constituencies and prepare for a loss of some of their seats.

But equally don't expect election speculation to subside at this conference.

Environmental campaigners are firmly opposed to Rosebank and Jackdaw

'Breathing space'

The Labour Party has tried and trusted methods of managing dissent at party conferences, when it comes to votes on party policy.

But the coming week could see a concerted effort by some on the left to push for a complete ban on arms sales to Israel and for Israel's actions in Gaza to be described by Labour as a genocide.

Those close to Burnham believe he has gained considerable credit by sanctioning the illegal Israeli settlements on the West Bank and won't need to go further.

There is also some frustration that his government has not yet revised proposals to make migrants wait much longer to gain permanent residency rights, and there are genuine differences over whether the Rosebank and Jackdaw oil and gas fields should go ahead.

But while Burnham is facing some difficult calls, this is not a leader facing a restless party in revolt.

He has offered to give the hard-pressed public "breathing space" amid a cost of living crisis.

And his own party is so far giving him breathing space as leader – largely sighing with relief that it is not Sir Keir Starmer who will be delivering the main address this year.

Senior Labour officials have hailed the forthcoming conference as an opportunity to "show voters a party that is boldly, confidently, and authentically Labour".

But not too far below the political radar, there are already demands from some in the wider Labour movement to prove it.

stories.body:
Iran took a combative tone, a new Venezuela is announced, and Ukraine’s president aims at the Kremlin’s coffers

The rubber hit the road this week at the UN general assembly at a time of global urgency, with the Middle East crisis reverberating through markets around the world, AI sparking existential concerns, and few signs of cooperation between the US and China in their great power rivalry.

World leaders have gathered in New York to make their feelings known, both at the podium and at crucial meetings on the sidelines. Amid the chaos of the politicking and background briefings, here is a selection of key points we saw on day two.

1. No bending the knee for Iran Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, balanced defiance against the US with an openness to dialogue, in an address that had been in doubt as it was unclear he would be issued a visa to enter the country. “We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists,” he said. “Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country.” Referring to the United States, Pezeshkian added: “Yes, they did hit us, but we did not bend the knee .” The US delegation walked out of the room. US delegation walks out during Iranian president’s UNGA speech At the podium, Pezeshkian held up images of children killed in the strike on a school in Minab , which a UN fact-finding mission had found “reasonable grounds” to say was carried out by the US. Despite Donald Trump’s earlier public musings on whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic”, the US president said there had been a “very good” meeting on the fate of the strait of Hormuz between Tehran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

2. Xi Jinping gives it a miss The biggest thing not happening at the UN general assembly could well be any involvement by Xi Jinping. Amid crises in Ukraine and the Middle East that have seen Beijing accused of being at best unhelpful, Donald Trump rolled out a 100ft red carpet to personally meet his counterpart at Joint Base Andrews instead of the White House, a move not seen for decades. The two will talk about AI, trade and Taiwan during a state dinner and tea, but China will be represented at the UNGA by vice-president Han Zheng. On his arrival, Xi said “our two countries should be partners rather than rivals”, according to state news agency Xinhua, and a modest extension of their trade truce was announced, but expectations of a big breakthrough are low. View image in fullscreen The red carpet is rolled out at Joint Base Andrews for China’s Xi Jinping. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

3. ‘Today, Venezuela is being reborn’ Venezuela’s interim president described the “rebirth” of her country, as she addressed for the UN for the first time since the abduction of her old boss on the orders of Trump. Delcy Rodríguez, speaking as Nicolás Maduro languished in a prison nearly in Brooklyn , promised elections at an undisclosed point in the future and said her government had started a “political dialogue with opposition sectors”. Earlier, she had watched as Trump defended the US intervention in her country, saying: “It was a war … [and] to the victor belong the spoils”, an allusion to the controversial 65bn-barrel oil deal she agreed, which the president called “the largest oil deal in history”. View image in fullscreen Acting President of Venezuela Delcy Rodríguez Photograph: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images

4. ‘Russia’s revenues must remain a target’ As the war grinds towards its fifth winter, Ukraine’s president was clear-eyed about how to hurt Russia: hit the Kremlin’s coffers. “Russia’s revenues must remain a target,” Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the assembly. “When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said. The president flagged that the upcoming winter could be “very harsh for us”, given the annual onslaught against its energy infrastructure, but warned that Kyiv could “make it painful for Russia too”. Ukraine has used long-range drones to strike Russian warehouses, ‌port infrastructure and oil refineries, but Trump has pressed Zelenskyy to “stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia” because it was causing a global shortage. Although Russian president Vladimir Putin is not at the UN, Trump has invited him to December’s G20 in Miami , which would mark a significant step in welcoming Putin back on to the world stage. 1:05 Zelenskyy at UN urges world leaders to end trade with Russia – video

5. Coming up ... Netanyahu New York is bracing for protests, both in the assembly hall and on the streets, when Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks on Thursday against a background of growing international condemnation, most recently over violence by Israeli settlers in the West Bank. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani told demonstrators this week he would protect their “right to [protest] in this city” but tempered his earlier promises to arrest Netanyahu as a war criminal. Palestinian representatives are calling for diplomatic missions to bring staff for a planned walkout of Netanyahu’s speech. Netanyahu is expected to deliver a hardline message aimed not just at world leaders, but also to his own electorate in Israel ahead of elections next month . Trump and top US officials are not expected to meet Netanyahu, but will be listening carefully to his words – 60% of American Jews in a poll released this week hope Netanyahu is voted out in October. stories.title: 'This is the final offer,' says NI secretary over £1.5bn Stormont funding package
stories.summary: Some six months have passed since the executive should have set a budget for this financial year.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Northern Ireland Secretary Chris Bryant, pictured in early September

Published 24 September 2026

The Northern Ireland Secretary of State has said the government's £1.5bn financial package for Stormont is his "final offer" and has given executive parties until next Thursday to respond.

Sir Chris Bryant said there was "no more money" available and that the Northern Ireland Executive needed to agree on a budget.

He said he would have to consider "every eventuality" if the executive failed to reach an agreement, including the possibility of a budget being passed at Westminster but wanted to "sit down and I'll be as cooperative as I possibly can".

However some parties have criticised the deadline with the DUP's Diane Dodds describing it as "reckless".

Earlier this month, Bryant made an offer of a financial package worth about £1.5bn over the next three years - that was a rise from an initial proposal of £1.1bn.

But executive parties said it did not go far enough and have argued that significant gaps remain before they can agree to a deal that would allow them to set a budget.

Some six months have passed since the executive should have set a budget for this financial year.

'There is no more money'

Speaking to BBC Newsline , Sir Chris said he had given executive parties until noon next Thursday to come back to him with a plan for agreeing a budget for this year and the following two years.

"It's my final offer. It's a good offer," he said.

He added: "There is no more money. The financial situation in the UK government at the moment is very, very tight."

Asked whether he was prepared to introduce a budget at Westminster if the executive did not accept the offer, Sir Chris said: "I've got to look at every eventuality. Of course I have. I've got to be responsible about this."

He said he did not want to legislate for a budget and would prefer to work with executive parties to reach an agreement.

"If it's impossible to set a budget through the executive, then somebody else will have to do it for them," he said, adding that he was "not at that stage yet".

Sir Chris also said the executive would have to consider raising additional revenue, but that it was not his job to tell ministers how to do so.

He said he had not specifically raised the introduction of water charges with executive parties.

Executive parties seek more funding

"We've been underfunded for over a decade, so how do we ever catch up," Kimmins told The View

Infrastructure Minister Liz Kimmins said Northern Ireland had been "underfunded for over a decade". , external

The NI Fiscal Council has found that Scotland and Wales are currently funded above their levels of assessed need while NI is at or slightly below its assessed funding need.

Speaking to BBC's The View programme , the Sinn Féin minister said: "The people here pay their taxes, they're entitled to good public services."

"We'll continue to stand up for that and ensure that message is heard loud and clear and I think the executive is united in that," she added.

Diane Dodds says the secretary of state's deadline is "reckless and unrealistic"

DUP MLA Diane Dodds described the Northern Ireland Secretary's final offer , external as "reckless" and "unrealistic".

"He needs to be honest with people in Northern Ireland. Is he....going to stand over the decimation of public services in Northern Ireland and severe cuts to those public services or is he going to be realistic and sit down with parties instead of haranguing people over the media on this issues," she told The View.

She said Sir Chris knew Northern Ireland was "underfunded relative to need and relative to other parts of the United Kingdom".

Executive parties have been in negotiations with the government in a bid to get increased funding.

Finance Minister John O'Dowd previously said the current published financial pressures facing Stormont departments were around £1.6bn, adding: "So we have a bit to go."

Northern Ireland Executive parties had rejected an initial £1.1bn package over three years

The Ulster Unionist Party (UUP)'s Steve Aiken said that "calling this the final offer does not make it a fair or sufficient offer".

"The UK government has moved significantly from its opening position, and that should be acknowledged. However, even with extensive savings, the annual funding on offer would barely meet the pressures in health alone. That puts the scale of the Executive's wider problem into stark perspective."

He said it had been made clear during meetings that public services need to "deliver to our citizens the same standard of health, education, policing and other services as is available in any other postcode in our nation".

The offer on the table from the government includes £450m extra for day-to-day pressures this year, as well as an additional £400m in 2027/28 and 2028/29.

stories.body:
President lays out red carpet as treasury secretary announces extension of ‘Busan agreement’ pausing trade war hostilities

AI, trade, Taiwan and climate: what will and won’t be on agenda at Trump-Xi summit

Donald Trump has welcomed Xi Jinping to the US, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to kick off his state visit to Washington.

Xi’s plane was met with a lavish arrival ceremony that included a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet flanked by US service members, a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries.

US presidents typically welcome foreign leaders at the White House, but Trump and the first lady, Melania, traveled to the the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, to personally shake hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, on Wednesday evening.

Xi’s visit comes as world leaders gather in New York for the United Nations general assembly , although the Chinese leader will not address the meeting. He has attended the UNGA just once since becoming president in 2012.

“It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is ⁠coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York,” Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters. “I think a lot of people will say: ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’”

Scott ⁠Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced that the US ⁠and ​China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan ⁠agreement – a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies.

Bessent, who met the Chinese ‌vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would be extended until 10 January, two months after it was due to expire.

The US and China have long been competing to develop increasingly powerful technology, but the race to further AI has become a major topic among tech companies – especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.

Trump has dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people, instead promoting more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last week.

The president and members of the administration have insisted that leading AI development also means leading the world militarily and economically – further raising the stakes for the US and China.

Xi’s visit is expected to be filled with ceremonial displays, reciprocating the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.

Trump’s decision to greet the Chinese leader at his plane, rather than at the White House, shows how far the US president is willing to go to honor Xi.

The revelation about the attempted suicides came in response to the fifth of the senator’s 12 questions. Here is the full text of the exchange:

double quotation mark 5. Have there been any suicides aboard the ship during this deployment? Since the beginning of LINCOLN’s deployment, there have been a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group - this number includes the LINCOLN crew and Sailors from the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers, and all embarked aviation squadrons.

In a statement to the Guardian, Gillibrand said: “What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as ‘ fake news ’ turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members. Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect. That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable.”

Here is the complete text of Cao’s response to Gillibrand’s questions:

The White House appeared to confirm on Wednesday night that what it called sensitive national security information on the Iran war published by Politico, which it pointed to this week as justification for Donald Trump banning the news outlet, was provided to the publication by vice-president JD Vance.

The White House statement was released in response to reporting on Wednesday from the media outlet Status, which identified Vance as the anonymous “senior administration official” quoted by Politico in a 12 June 2026 article on the progress of US talks with Iran.

“Indeed, Vance not only briefed POLITICO on the state of the Iran deal talks, but spoke to a group of reporters from several news organizations”, Status reported . “In exchange for the information, those outlets agreed to grant Vance anonymity.”

A social media post from the White House then seemed to acknowledge Vance was the source for what the White House had called, in a letter to Politico on Tuesday, an article with “sensitive security information, and misinformation about national security information” so reckless that it justified the news outlet being banned from covering Trump in person.

A US district judge on Wednesday heard arguments in the extraordinary showdown between Donald Trump and CNN, MS Now and Politico, suggesting in comments that he was more inclined to side with the media plaintiffs who sued the president on Monday.

The three news organizations were not given advance notice that they were in violation of any set of standards and only received formal notice – in letters sent to each news organization on Tuesday – that they “exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information”.

stories.title: New York defies Trump admin, asks court to shut down Polymarket gambling

stories.body:
New York sues Polymarket as Trump admin tries to override state gambling laws.

New York sued Polymarket today, alleging that it runs an “illegal gambling operation” through its prediction market.

“By running an unlicensed gambling operation, Polymarket has done more than just knowingly violate state law, they have put New Yorkers at risk, especially those underage who are most vulnerable to problem gaming,” Governor Kathy Hochul said in a press release announcing the lawsuit.

Polymarket is “sidestepping its obligation to pay taxes like licensed casinos and mobile sports gambling platforms do,” New York said. “This tax revenue from gambling regulation funds public schools, sports programs for underserved youth, and problem gambling education and treatment.”

Polymarket is “available to users between the ages of 18–20, even though New York law requires a person to be at least 21 years old to participate in mobile sports betting,” exposing young people to gambling’s “damaging effects on their mental and financial well-being,” New York said.

New York previously sued Kalshi, Polymarket’s chief rival. The Trump administration is on the side of the prediction markets, with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) asserting exclusive jurisdiction over the platforms. In August, the CFTC declared a “market emergency” in New York in an attempt to stop the state from applying its gambling laws to Kalshi.

Gambling with a different name

Polymarket and its rival Kalshi offer sports bets in the form of “event contracts” or “swaps,” which state governments and some courts say are just gambling with a different name.

“Our gambling laws exist to protect New Yorkers, prevent the potential harms of problem gambling, and ensure funding for educational and public benefit programs,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said. “By skirting New York’s laws, Polymarket is targeting the most vulnerable and depriving New York families of critical services and support.”

The New York press release said the state government is “seeking a court order stopping Polymarket from operating as an unlicensed gambling business and requiring the company to pay fines, forfeit all illegal gains and pay restitution to users.” The lawsuit was filed today in a New York County court.

Polymarket’s main platform technically hasn’t been available in the US since 2022, when the CFTC ruled it was an illegally unregistered exchange. Polymarket’s website is restricted to view-only mode in the US, though users can get around that with a virtual private network. Polymarket promoted its platform in the US with a campaign that paid dozens of social media users to film themselves making fake bets on copies of the Polymarket website, The Wall Street Journal reported in June .

Polymarket is seeking the CFTC’s permission to bring its main exchange back to the US, but it was able to launch a more limited, mobile-app version in December 2025 after acquiring QCX, a CFTC-licensed firm. The New York lawsuit was filed against QCX LLC, also known as Polymarket US.

NY alleges “flagrant disregard” of state law

While Kentucky sued Polymarket in June, most of the court cases over state regulation of prediction markets have involved Kalshi. States including New York have sued Kalshi, and Kalshi sued other states after receiving cease-and-desist orders commanding it to stop offering gambling.

Polymarket “seeks to avoid the legal and financial consequences of New York’s close regulation of gambling by offering what is quintessentially wagering under the guise of ‘event contracts’ on a ‘prediction market,’” the New York lawsuit said. “Respondent accepts wagers from members of the public as a gambling business in New York in flagrant disregard of New York’s State Constitution, penal laws, and other statutes. Respondent is not licensed with the New York State Gaming Commission in any capacity.”

The lawsuit against Polymarket closely mirrors the one that New York filed against Kalshi in July. Polymarket provided Ars with a statement today in response to what it called a “copy/paste” lawsuit:

Polymarket was founded in a tiny NYC apartment and now has more than 350 employees here, embodying why people and businesses come here to make it. We believe in New York and we’re staying here. While the AG’s decision to copy/paste a recycled lawsuit is disappointing, we’ll fight for our users. We didn’t run to preemptively sue the state—we chose to engage with them directly on the substance and address their concerns. They preferred the media hit. Any time the AG’s office wants to swing by, our door is open for a conversation about how we protect consumers and offer fair, transparent, and legal markets.

Supreme Court may decide matter for all states

New York’s lawsuit said Polymarket’s offering meets the legal definition of gambling under state law. A person “engages in gambling when he stakes or risks something of value upon the outcome of a contest of chance or a future contingent event not under his control or influence, upon an agreement or understanding that he will receive something of value in the event of a certain outcome,” the state law says.

The lawsuit said examples of bets offered by Polymarket include whether the Green Bay Packers would win a football game against the New York Giants, who would win the Super Bowl in February 2026, and who would win college basketball games such as the March 20, 2026 contest between Hofstra University and the University of Alabama.

The Supreme Court may ultimately decide whether states can restrict or prohibit sports gambling on prediction markets. While the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled that New Jersey cannot regulate sports bets on prediction markets, the Ninth Circuit appeals court ruled that Nevada can stop Kalshi from allowing sports bets.

The circuit courts disagree on whether a sports bet on a prediction market meets the federal definition of a “swap,” which can only be regulated by the CFTC. New Jersey recently urged the Supreme Court to settle the matter once and for all. “Companies like Kalshi claim to offer legal sports betting in all 50 states, but they refuse to follow the gambling laws of any state,” New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said at the time.

Published 24 September 2026

Pet owners will not have to pay a fee to own a dog, after the government ruled out introducing a licensing scheme.

In a report, published on Thursday, , external a panel of animal experts suggested the government should consider new legal requirements for dog owners.

The panel did not reach an agreement on which rules should be adopted but the taskforce said any new laws should aim to promote better dog control, reduce the risk of dog attacks and avoid placing an "undue burden" on owners.

A spokesperson for the environment department said: "This is a welcome report and ministers are considering the taskforce's recommendations, however we will not be introducing a new dog licensing scheme."

The Dog Control Coalition - which includes the RSPCA, Battersea Dogs & Cats Home and the Royal Kennel Club - said it supported the recommendations in the report and that it was "vital" for the government to take action "as a matter of urgency".

A spokesperson for the coalition said: "Dog bite incidents continue to have serious consequences for people and dogs, and the time that has passed since the publication of The Middlesex Report, in 2021, makes it imperative that we now see progress."

The report made 20 recommendations including calling for councils to provide a service to tackle low-level dog control issues, improved recording of dog bite wounds and legal requirements for dog walkers.

Dog attacks are still rising - even after the XL bully ban Published 30 April

What are the rules for having an XL bully dog? Published 24 March 2025

Dog licences explored to tackle ownership issues Published 7 May

The Responsible Dog Ownership Taskforce was established by the government in 2022, following a series of high-profile dog attacks.

The taskforce's report noted that since 2011 the dog population in the UK had grown by 35%, while hospital admissions relating to dog bites in England had risen by 77%.

It said pet ownership had spiked during the Covid pandemic at a time when it was harder to access support services.

"This led to less experienced owners struggling to access services and finding it harder to get help," the report said.

Until 1987, dog owners in England, Wales and Scotland had to pay an annual fee to get an ownership licence.

The scheme was scrapped on the grounds that the amount of money it raised was outweighed by the operating costs.

Dog owners in Northern Ireland still have to buy a licence of £12.50, or £5 if the owner receives an income-related benefit.

In France, owners of the most dangerous dogs have to get special permits which can involve passing a training course and putting the dog through a behavioural assessment.

Switzerland previously required potential dog owners to complete a knowledge test, followed by a practical, but this condition has been scrapped.

The report said that most members of the taskforce backed introducing legal requirements for dog owners but "further consideration would be needed regarding the form that this should take".

"Any legal requirement would need careful consideration of its objective and not appear as a tax on already responsible dog owners.

"Reintroducing a universal dog licence may amount to another database of responsible owners or an administrative exercise with little public safety benefit or opportunity to promote responsible dog ownership."

It said options could include focusing a scheme on high-risk dogs, introducing background checks on owners and requiring potential owners to pass a knowledge test.

The Dogs Trust and the RSPCA have commissioned research into the costs and benefits of different systems and their conclusions are due to be published later this year.

In a ministerial foreword to the report, environment minister Baroness Hayman of Ullock said: "In recent years, we have seen a concerning rise in dog attacks, alongside changes in patterns of dog ownership."

She said the taskforce's report was an "important and timely contribution", adding: "As ministers, we are carefully considering the recommendations alongside the wider programme of work already under way."

Published 24 September 2026

The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.

Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".

The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.

Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.

The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles.

"Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday , external .

"Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."

His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.

Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does."

"Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.

Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.

This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".

Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".

Many of the Elgin Marbles originate from the Parthenon in Athens

British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century.

They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens.

After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament.

The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal.

The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum.

Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years.

Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again.

Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces.

The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common.

Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority.

stories.title: Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
stories.summary: Andy Burnham has long championed a repeal of the ban which prevents football supporters from drinking alcohol in the view of the pitch. But do fans even want it?
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The law permits supporters at stadiums from the Premier League to National League to drink alcohol outside the ground and in concourses, but not in their seats

Published 24 September 2026

When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds.

Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated.

It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm.

"I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events.

There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule.

That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street.

It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But is it something that match-going supporters actually want?

What the law says

Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985.

It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s.

The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch.

Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch.

The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans.

It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden.

However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons.

It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership.

The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month.

The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football.

The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change.

Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power?

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought".

The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation".

It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding".

Fans' views differ on drinking in stands

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Should alcohol be allowed in football stands?

The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law.

Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans.

"I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.

"If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable.

"It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats."

The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol.

Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all.

Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion.

The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important.

It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream.

The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does.

Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing.

Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine" .

"[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said.

"Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established.

"There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way."

Scottish football has slowly started to relax the ban of alcohol sales at matches but fans continue to protest for this to move at a faster pace.

For many match-going fans, however, the prospect of beer being thrown and potential anti-social behaviour outweighs the opportunity to watch a game with a pint.

Dave, a Chelsea fan from Twickenham, told Nicky Campbell on BBC Radio 5 Live, that he was "100% against it".

"Have a look at some of the footage you see on social media at Boxpark, for instance. A goal goes in and there is beer and lager thrown everywhere," he said.

"I don't want to go round stinking of other people's beer and there is a fashion among certain supporters to throw their beer everywhere.

"If people can't go without drink for a 45-minute period there is something the matter with them."

Adrian, from Leicester, claimed it would be the "worst idea you could come up with".

"There is enough trouble with other things in football, with the flares, drug taking and other things," he added. "You throw the alcohol in as well. Football is tribal whereas other sports they aren't."

But Ryan, a Wolves fan in Banbury, said "a solution that suits everybody" is to provide designated areas for drinking in stands.

What is it like in other sports and different countries?

Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol.

Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football.

The restrictions differ around Europe.

There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats.

In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds.

In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium.

In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas.
